narrative:
After carefully reviewing your application, the admissions system flagged a significant concern about your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, estimating a 51% probability of failure — a figure that, while close to the borderline, was just enough to result in a rejection decision. Your profile tells a nuanced story, and it is important that you understand exactly what drove this outcome and where the system saw both strengths and weaknesses in your candidacy.

The single most influential factor in this decision was your academic performance during your third year of law school, where your grades placed you in the 1st decile within your school — meaning you ranked among the lowest-performing students in your cohort at that stage. Students who successfully pass the bar exam on their first try average around the 6th decile in their third year, so this gap is substantial and was the strongest signal the system used when assessing your application. Third-year performance is particularly telling because it reflects how well a student has consolidated their legal knowledge heading into the bar exam, and unfortunately, your standing here raised serious concerns.

That said, your profile is not without meaningful strengths, and the system did recognize them. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is notably higher than the average of 3.24 among students who passed the bar, and this worked meaningfully in your favor, partially counteracting the concern raised by your third-year standing. Similarly, your LSAT score of 34, while somewhat below the average of 37.27 among successful students, also contributed positively to your predicted outcome — suggesting that your aptitude, as measured before law school, was not a primary source of concern.

What makes your situation particularly complex is that despite these genuine strengths in your undergraduate record and aptitude scores, your in-school performance trajectory — especially the steep drop to the 1st decile by your third year, compared to a 3rd decile standing in your first year — appears to have been the deciding factor. Studying part-time, which only about 7% of students who passed the bar did, may also reflect pressures on your time and focus that could have contributed to this academic trajectory.

As a next step, we strongly encourage you to speak directly with an academic advisor or admissions counselor who can review your full record in context. Focusing on strengthening your academic standing, exploring bar preparation resources, and potentially retaking the LSAT could meaningfully improve your prospects in a future application cycle.
